reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett / ATS-IDSA NTM guidance
clinicalPearls: A slow-growing scotochromogen widely known as the tap water bacillus and the least pathogenic of the commonly encountered nontuberculous mycobacteria
One of the most frequent environmental and laboratory contaminants, so a positive culture is far more often contamination than infection
Recovered readily from tap water, laboratory water, and reagents, and a recognised cause of pseudo-outbreaks traced to contaminated water or solutions
Genuine disease is very rare and largely confined to severely immunocompromised patients or infection associated with prosthetic material and foreign bodies
Reported true infections include disseminated disease, pulmonary disease, and device-related infection
Diagnosis of real disease demands repeated isolation from a normally sterile or clinically compatible site and rigorous exclusion of contamination
Most single isolates require no treatment; when genuine infection is confirmed, macrolide-based multidrug therapy and removal of infected foreign material are used
reference.pathophysiology: Mycobacterium gordonae is a slow-growing scotochromogenic mycobacterium ubiquitous in water, including treated tap water, and a common contaminant of specimens, laboratory water, and reagents. Its very low virulence means that in immunocompetent people isolation almost always reflects colonisation or contamination rather than infection. Genuine disease is confined largely to hosts with severe impairment of cell-mediated immunity or to infection of prosthetic material and indwelling devices, where biofilm formation allows persistence. Because pseudo-outbreaks from contaminated water and solutions are well described, apparent clusters warrant investigation of the water supply and laboratory processes.
additionalDifferentials: Specimen or laboratory contamination (by far the most common explanation)
Disseminated infection from another opportunistic organism
Pseudo-outbreak from a contaminated water source
additionalInvestigations: Repeated cultures from a compatible or normally sterile site to establish genuine infection
Investigation of water supplies, reagents, and laboratory processes when a pseudo-outbreak is suspected
Assessment of immune status when true disease is considered
Imaging or device sampling in suspected prosthesis-related infection
Histological confirmation of organisms in tissue to support true infection
redFlags: Prosthesis- or device-related infection requiring removal
Clustered isolates indicating a contaminated water source or pseudo-outbreak
Repeated isolation from a normally sterile site
reference.prognosis: The clinical significance of most isolates is negligible and no treatment is needed. The rare instances of true infection occur in vulnerable hosts or around foreign material and depend on immune status and adequate source control; with these addressed, outcomes are generally acceptable.
pitfalls: Treating a single positive culture as infection when it almost always represents contamination
Missing a laboratory or water-source pseudo-outbreak
Failing to remove infected prosthetic material when genuine infection is confirmed
Subjecting patients to unnecessary prolonged toxic therapy for a contaminant
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
ATS/IDSA guideline on nontuberculous mycobacterial diseases
management: Recognise that most isolates represent contamination or colonisation and require no antimicrobial treatment
Establish genuine infection before treating by demanding repeated isolation from a normally sterile or clinically compatible site with histological confirmation of organisms in tissue
For confirmed true disease, use susceptibility-guided multidrug antimycobacterial therapy such as rifampicin, ethambutol, and a macrolide, sometimes with a fluoroquinolone
Achieve source control by removing infected prosthetic material or indwelling devices, where biofilm sustains infection
Investigate the water supply, reagents, and laboratory processes when a pseudo-outbreak is suspected
Assess and optimise immune status, since real disease occurs almost exclusively in the severely immunocompromised
Refer to infectious diseases, with outcomes generally acceptable once immune status and source control are addressed
